questions.prompt: Which command shows the changes you've staged for the next commit?
questions.explanation: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index (unstaged changes); `--staged` compares the index with HEAD, i.e. what would be committed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `git merge main` and `git rebase main` on a feature branch?
questions.answer: Merge adds a merge commit and keeps history as it happened; rebase replays your commits on top of main as new commits, giving linear history
distractors: Rebase deletes main's new commits from your branch
Merge rewrites your branch's commit hashes; rebase leaves them alone
They produce identical history; rebase is just faster
questions.explanation: Both end up with the same code. Rebase rewrites your commits (new hashes) so history reads as if you started from the latest main; merge preserves the real branching.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't you rebase commits that others have already pulled from a shared branch?
questions.answer: Rebase replaces them with new commits (new hashes), so anyone who built on the old ones ends up with diverged, duplicated history, and you have to force-push
distractors: Git refuses to rebase commits that have been pushed
Rebasing pushed commits deletes them from the remote immediately
Rebase only works on commits that exist locally
questions.explanation: Rewriting is fine on your own unpublished branch. On shared history, use merge or revert, which only add commits.

questions.prompt: Which command safely undoes a commit that's already been pushed, by adding a new commit that reverses it?
questions.explanation: revert adds history instead of removing it, so nobody else's clone breaks. reset moves your branch backwards, which needs a force-push once the commit is shared.

questions.answer: Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
distractors: Undoes the last commit and keeps its changes in the working tree, unstaged
Undoes the last commit and throws its changes away
Adds a new commit that reverses the last one
questions.explanation: --soft moves the branch only; --mixed (the default) also resets the index, leaving the changes unstaged; --hard resets the working tree too, discarding them.

questions.prompt: Which command shelves your uncommitted changes so you can switch branches with a clean working tree, and bring them back later?
questions.explanation: `git stash` saves the changes on a stack and cleans the working tree; `git stash pop` reapplies them. `git checkout -- .` would just discard them.

questions.prompt: What is a "detached HEAD" in git?
questions.answer: HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch, so new commits belong to no branch and are easy to lose when you switch away
distractors: The remote branch you were tracking has been deleted
A merge or rebase stopped halfway with conflicts
HEAD points at a branch with no commits yet
questions.explanation: Checking out a tag or a commit hash detaches HEAD. That's fine for looking around; to keep work done there, create a branch (`git switch -c name`).

questions.prompt: Which git command finds the commit that introduced a bug by binary searching through history?
questions.explanation: Mark one good and one bad commit and bisect checks out the midpoint each time; `git bisect run <test>` automates it. blame shows who last changed each line, not when the behaviour broke.

questions.prompt: Which command lists everywhere HEAD has pointed recently, so you can recover commits "lost" after a reset or a bad rebase?
questions.explanation: The reflog is a local history of HEAD movements. Find the hash from before the mistake and `git reset --hard` to it (or branch from it).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
questions.answer: fetch downloads new commits and updates the remote-tracking branches only; pull is a fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch
distractors: fetch updates your working tree; pull only downloads
fetch downloads branch names only, not commits
They're aliases for the same command
questions.explanation: Fetching is always safe: it never touches your branches or files. Fetch first and inspect `origin/main` if you want to see what a pull would bring in.

questions.prompt: Which command changes the message (or adds staged changes to) the most recent commit?
questions.explanation: --amend replaces the last commit with a new one. It's a rewrite, so don't amend a commit you've already pushed to a shared branch.

questions.prompt: Which `git push` option force-pushes only if the remote branch is still where you last saw it, refusing if someone else pushed in the meantime?
questions.explanation: Plain --force overwrites whatever is on the remote, including a colleague's new commits. --force-with-lease checks first.

questions.answer: When the target branch hasn't moved since you branched, git just moves its pointer up to your latest commit: no merge commit
distractors: A merge that skips running the hooks
A merge that squashes all your commits into one
A merge that automatically resolves conflicts in your favour
questions.explanation: There's nothing to combine, so the history stays linear. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit anyway, to record that a branch existed.
